panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 9 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I). A: Microscopic view of the solid component of the pancreatic tumor, consistent with SPN. B: Visibly demonstrates the pseudopapillary arrangement characteristic of SPN. C: Shows intra-tumor hemorrhage and necrosis. D: Shows liver metastasis with increased cellular atypia compared to the primary tumor. E: Immunohistochemical evidence showing nuclear $\beta$-catenin expression in the tumor. F: Prophylactic proliferation index (Ki-67) observed in the tumor. G: Gross presentation of a larger pancreatic mass showing mixed cystic/solid components and a fibrous pseudocapsule. H: Gross specimen of a smaller pancreatic mass lacking a distinct fibrous envelope or obvious cysts. I: Gross appearance of hepatic metastases exhibiting heterogeneous color and cystic cavities.

Histopathology revealed a neoplasm composed of monomorphic polygonal cells arranged in solid sheets and pseudopapillary structures. Hyalinized stroma and focal necrosis were present (Figure 3). Immunohistochemical staining showed strong nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity for β‐catenin, as well as positive staining for SOX11 and androgen receptor (AR). A: Multi-planar CT images (including axial view A) demonstrating a large, well-defined mass in the pancreatic head/retroperitoneum, consistent with the radiologist's reported diagnosis of Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm, showing mixed solid/cystic characteristics. B: Coronal CT reconstruction (Panel B) displays the retroperitoneal mass characteristic of Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm, showing expected heterogeneous appearance and mixed enhancement. C: Sagittal CT reconstruction (Panel C) of the mass in the pancreas/retroperitoneum, confirming the location and extent of the lesion suggestive of Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm.

in_text_mentions: 7.2 cm in height. The lesion contained solid, cystic, and calcified components. It was in close contact with the duodenum, the splenomesenteric confluence, and the right colic flexure, without evidence of invasion (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a large pancreatic head mass measuring 12 × 7.7 cm. The tumor showed mixed solid, cystic, and calcified components. It abutted the right colic flexure and the inferior vena cava, without biliary or pancreatic ductal dilatation. Overall, the imaging findings were most suggestive of a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel (a) shows histology demonstrating monomorphic cells with solid and pseudopapillary architecture mixed with hyalinized stroma, meeting criteria for solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. b: Panel (b) shows immunohistochemical staining for nuclear beta-catenin, which was strongly positive, supporting the diagnosis of solid pseudopapillary neoplasm.

panels.figure_caption: (a) Monomorphic cells with solid and pseudopapillary architecture admixed with hyalinized to myxoid stroma. (b) Immunochemical stain for β-catenin nuclear was strongly positive. The β-catenin staining was done using a Ventana Benchmark Ultra Instrument and the Ventana Optiview DAB staining kit. The antibody was Clone 14 from Ventana Medical Systems (Oro Valley, Arizona, USA).
in_text_mentions: On microscopic examination (Figure 3(a)), the tumor was found to be composed of monomorphic cells with solid and pseudopapillary architecture mixed with hyalinized to myxoid stroma with degeneration and dystrophic calcification. Some of the tumor cells had eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm. Necrosis or high-nuclear-grade atypia was not seen, though mitotic figures were present.

Immunohistochemistry revealed the tumor to be positive for nuclear β-catenin (Figure 3(b)) and low molecular keratin Cam 5.2. It was focally positive for progesterone receptor (PR) but negative for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and estrogen receptor (ER) (data not shown). The Cam 5.2, PR, ER, synaptophysin, and chromogranin antibodies were also obtained from Ventana and developed with the same system as the β-catenin.

A: H&E stain of the pancreatic body lesion showing diffuse epithelioid proliferation with a hepatoid pattern, consistent with the described SPN variant. in_text_mentions: tems) with a slow‐pull technique. Rapid on‐site evaluation with quick Papanicolaou staining was performed. Adequate diagnostic material consisting of atypical cells with nuclear enlargement was confirmed, and therefore, the procedure was completed after two passes. Tissue specimens stained with hematoxylin and eosin revealed diffuse epithelioid proliferation involving polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm (Figure 2a). These cells exhibited a hepatoid pattern, closely resembling hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Prominent nucleoli, anisokaryosis, and focal necrosis were also noted.

Immunohistochemically, HepPar‐1 (Figure 2b) and CD10 (Figure 2c) were diffusely positive, supporting hepatoid differentiation. The tumor cells were also positive for AE1/AE3 and CD56 but negative for CK7, CK20, CD34, IMP3, and CEA. No neuroendocrine markers, including chromogranin A and synaptophysin, were seen. Furthermore, β‐catenin clearly accumulated in the nucleus—a characteristic feature of SPN (Figure 2d). The Ki‐67 labeling index was below 1%. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is the unenhanced phase showing the solid-cystic pancreatic mass architecture of SPN, including internal hyperattenuating areas suggesting hemorrhage, which matches the described lesion. B: Panel B is the arterial phase, showing the characteristic enhancement of a solid-cystic SPN, and the hyperattenuating area of possible hemorrhage. C: Panel C is the venous phase, demonstrating the mild heterogeneous enhancement typical of the SPN mass. D: Panel D is the delayed phase, continuing to show the SPN mass characteristics and associated intratumoral hemorrhage.

in_text_mentions: t axial section. On the unenhanced images, the lesion was internally heterogeneous and contained relatively hyperattenuating areas. The non-cystic component showed mild heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. The descending duodenum was compressed and displaced, without an infiltrative margin. In view of the patient's age and sex, the circumscribed margin, cystic and solid architecture, internal hemorrhagic appearance, and enhancement pattern, SPN was the leading imaging consideration. Pancreatic pseudocyst and other pancreatic neoplasms were considered less likely (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: showed a neoplasm of the head of the pancreas, with a solid and cyst appearance, and abundant haemorrhagic content. The neoplasm extended to the duodenum, causing fistulation to the lumen (Fig. 4). The immunohistochemical study showed expression of β-catenin, synaptophysin, vimentin and progesterone receptor (15%) and negativity for chromogranin, E-cadherin and CD117 (Fig. 5). The labelling index of Ki 67 was 2%, and the final diagnosis was a T3N0M0 SPN. The patient did not receive postoperative chemotherapy and has remained symptom-free with no detectable recurrence for 2 years of follow-up.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a cytology smear (Papanicolaou-stained) of pancreatic tissue showing hemorrhagic background and tissue fragments, consistent with the presentation of SPN. B: Panel B shows the classic pseudopapillary architecture of SPN in a Papanicolaou-stained smear. C: Panel C displays the cytomorphological features of SPN, including degenerative hemorrhage and specific cellular characteristics, within a cytology smear. D: Panel D highlights the high-power view of SPN, demonstrating the pseudopapillary structure as described in the caption.

Pancreatic Collision Tumor Composed of Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm and Well-Differentiated Neuroendocrine Tumor: Diagnostic Challenges and Classification Considerations.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112580. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Cytomorphologic features of pancreatic solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) on Papanicolaou-stained endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) smears. (A) Low-power Papanicolaou-stained smear demonstrating a moderately cellular specimen composed of numerous delicate tissue fragments in a hemorrhagic background (4× objective). (B) Papanicolaou-stained smear showing characteristic pseudopapillary architecture with loosely cohesive monomorphic neoplastic cells attached to delicate fibrovascular cores (20× objective). (C) Papanicolaou-stained smear demonstrating uniform tumor cells with round to oval nuclei, delicate cytoplasm, focal hyaline globules, and a degenerative hemorrhagic background (20× objective). (D) High-power Papanicolaou-stained smear showing monomorphic neoplastic cells lining delicate fibrovascular stalks with focal discohesion, imparting the characteristic pseudopapillary appearance of SPN (40× objective).
in_text_mentions: One month later, endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed, irregular pancreatic neck mass measuring 3.7 × 2.4 cm (Figure 2). The lesion abutted the portal venous confluence and hepatic artery without vascular encasement, luminal irregularity, or stenosis. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) showed a neoplasm immunoreactive for β-catenin and CD10, with focal synaptophysin and chromogranin expression and negative mucicarmine staining, supporting a diagnosis of solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN). Based on these findings, surgical resection was pursued (Figure 3).

as approximately 12 cm in the greatest dimension and had a mixed signal intensity with both solid and cystic elements. Internal fluid-fluid levels were noted, indicating hemorrhagic or necrotic changes in the mass. Areas of hyperintensity were noted peripherally, and the lesion was observed displacing neighboring structures, including the pancreas and stomach. The yellow arrow, as shown in Figure 2B, indicates the epicenter of the mass, which was one of the factors making the diagnosis difficult because the lesion simulated the appearance of an ovarian or gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

An axial MRI of the abdomen revealed an enlarged, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass circled in yellow in Figure 2C, anterior to the left kidney and next to the distal pancreas. The mass showed a mixed signal intensity with prominent solid and fluid-filled areas. Hyperintensity within the lesion indicated hemorrhagic or necrotic changes, and internal fluid-fluid levels were noted. The mass displaced the overlying structures, including the stomach and pancreas, without causing invasion.

Contrast-enhanced harmonic endoscopic ultrasound (CH-EUS) revealed hyperechoic solid granular components interspersed with small anechoic regions within the pancreatic mass ( Fig. 3 ). These characteristics were typical of the “alveolus nest sign” and were present during the arterial and venous phases of CH-EUS ( Video 1 ). in_text_mentions: h an operative duration of 199 min. Blood loss during the surgery was 5350 mL, and the patient received a red blood cell transfusion of 3160 mL. She was discharged on postoperative day 13. Histological examination revealed that the tumor consisted of small, uniform neoplastic epithelial cells with papillary structures and myxedematous stroma (Fig. 4). No vascular invasion was observed. Immunohistochemistry showed positive results for β-catenin, CD10, CD56, and synaptophysin, while chromogranin A was negative. The Ki-67 labeling index was 1%–2%. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with an SPN.

The pathological analysis confirmed the metastatic nature of the SPN as capsular with very few capsular and vascular invasions ( Figure 2 ). Grossly, the cross-section of the peritoneal metastatic tumor revealed a round, well demarcated mass measuring 75 × 50 mm that consisted of a mixed component containing focal hemorrhage. The tumor showed nested-to-diffuse growth of more poorly cohesive monomorphic cells with scattered nuclear atypia and fibrovascular stalks in which mitosis was sparse with the Ki-67 index 5-10%. In the late lesions, malignant histological features, such as peritumoral infiltration into the fat tissue (from the fourth lesion) and the organ, prominent capsular and vascular invasion were observed ( Figures 2A, B ). in_text_mentions: This case involves a 23-year-old primigravida patient at 25 weeks of gestation who presented with recurrent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. The clinical and radiological investigations revealed a large mass in the epigastric region, which was initially suspected to be of ovarian origin (such as ovarian torsion). However, the definitive diagnosis was made following surgery and histopathological analysis, revealing an SPN of the pancreas (Figure 1).

Additional immunohistochemical examination demonstrated that the tumor cells were positive for CD10, vimentin, progesterone receptor (PR), and neuron-specific enolase (NSE), and the low Ki-67 index indicated minimal proliferative activity. Notably, neuroendocrine and ovarian tumor markers were absent, proving that this neoplasm was of pancreatic origin, despite its aberrant site (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H). A: Panel A provides a T1-weighted MRI showing a mass with T1 hyperintensity, indicative of hemorrhage, consistent with SPN. B: Panel B displays a T2-weighted MRI image demonstrating marked internal heterogeneity of the pancreatic head mass. C: Panel C shows a diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequence demonstrating restricted diffusion in the mass. D: Panel D shows the ADC map with measurement ROI indicating restricted diffusion, typically associated with solid masses. E: Panel E is the arterial phase MRI showing the pancreatic mass exhibiting post-contrast enhancement. F: Panel F is the venous phase MRI showing the mass demonstrates post-contrast enhancement. G: Panel G is a coronal venous-phase reconstruction showing the pancreatic mass enhancement. H: Panel H is the delayed phase MRI showing the continued enhancement of the pancreatic mass.

panels.figure_caption: Multiparametric and contrast-enhanced MRI of the pancreatic head mass A: T1-weighted image showing peripheral and internal intrinsic T1 hyperintensity compatible with blood products; B: T2-weighted image showing marked internal heterogeneity; C: DWI; D: ADC map with the measurement ROI; E: arterial phase; F: venous phase; G: coronal venous-phase reconstruction; H: delayed phase. A non-cystic portion shows mild to moderate post-contrast enhancement, and the capsule enhances. Restricted diffusion and the ADC measurement are not specific for viable tumor, because clotted blood products may also restrict diffusion. The white arrow indicates the tumor, while the green arrow indicates a crescent-shaped area of T1 hyperintensity, suggestive of intratumoral hemorrhage, as blood products commonly exhibit high signal intensity on unenhanced T1-weighted images MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; DWI: diffusion-weighted imaging; ADC: apparent diffusion coefficient; ROI: region of interest

DWI demonstrated restricted diffusion in a non-cystic portion of the lesion that also showed post-contrast enhancement, with a measured ADC of approximately 0.98 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. The non-cystic component showed mild to moderate enhancement, and the capsule enhanced. Because blood products may alter DWI signal and ADC measurements, the DWI and ADC findings were interpreted together with the conventional and post-contrast images rather than being used alone to define viable tumor tissue. in_text_mentions: A 33-year-old woman was referred to Kansai Medical University following the detection of liver dysfunction during a routine medical checkup. CECT revealed a well-demarcated, hypovascular tumor measuring 20 mm in diameter in the pancreatic body (Fig. 1A and 1B). The internal heterogeneity of the tumor was suggestive of intratumoral hemorrhage. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, along with slight dilatation of the distal pancreatic duct. DWI showed high signal intensity at the corresponding site (Fig. 1C and 1D).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: This is a gross photograph of a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the ovary, showing its heterogeneous nature with cystic and solid components. B: H&E low power view showing the neoplasm arising within the ovarian tissue. C: H&E view highlighting the complex architecture and transition zones of the neoplasm. D: H&E view showing the transition zone and lack of sharp margins between tumor and normal tissue. in_text_mentions: can occur in all parts of the pancreas, there is a slight predilection for the pancreatic tail [6]. The wall of the lesions is smooth in the majority of cases, but it can also be nodular [20]. On T1-weighted images, the internal content is hypointense, but usually with hyperintense areas due to internal hemorrhage [20]. On T2-weighted images, the most common appearance is heterogeneously hyperintense. Typically, a solid component enhances poorly in comparison to the rest of the pancreas in the arterial phase with a progressive enhancement in the portal-venous and delayed phase [11] (Figure 1).

panels.figure_caption: Abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT) with an abdominal window A well-defined cystic lesion was identified in the tail of the pancreas (red "*"), visualized on coronal (Figure 1a), sagittal (Figure 1b), and axial (Figure 1c) planes on contrast-enhanced CT in the venous phase. It demonstrated homogeneous low attenuation after contrast administration, without an apparent solid component (27 Hounsfield units); an unenhanced phase was not performed. The lesion measured approximately 68.1 × 56 mm in its largest dimensions. A small amount of free fluid was noted in the left paracolic gutter (Figure 1c). No other significant findings were identified.

in_text_mentions: The patient underwent robotic distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy. On gross examination, the specimen weighed 599 g. Serial sectioning of the pancreas revealed a well-circumscribed lesion located in the distal portion, measuring 6.5 × 5.5 × 5.5 cm. The cut surface of the mass was heterogeneous, displaying tan-yellow areas, foci of hemorrhage, light brown fleshy zones, and white calcified regions, reflecting the mixed gross and microscopic appearance characteristic of this tumor (Figure 7). The lesion was found abutting the splenic capsule, which appeared focally disrupted.

plate_findings.evidence: neoplasm composed of poorly cohesive cells arranged in pseudopapillary structures

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 10 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J). A: Histology (H&E) showing characteristic pseudopapillary structure, supporting the diagnosis of solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. B: H&E micrograph showing uniform tumor cell morphology consistent with a well-differentiated neoplasm. C: IHC for β-catenin showing activation (nuclear/cytoplasmic positivity), a known characteristic of this neoplasm. D: IHC for alpha-1-antitrypsin showing diffuse cytoplasmic positivity. E: IHC for CD56 showing membranous positivity. F: IHC for Progesterone receptor showing nuclear positivity. G: IHC for chromogranin negative staining, which is helpful in excluding differential diagnoses. H: IHC for CK7 showing negative staining. I: IHC for synaptophysin negative staining. J: IHC for CD10 showing membranous positivity.
panels.attribution_text: Abarca Ruiz et al. Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm of the Pancreatic Head With Atypical Presentation in a Young Woman: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.108133. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of the tumor (A) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), 10× magnification, showing a neoplasm composed of poorly cohesive cells arranged in pseudopapillary structures with delicate fibrovascular cores; (B) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), 40× magnification, demonstrating relatively uniform tumor cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei, consistent with a well-differentiated neoplasm; (C) Immunohistochemistry for β-catenin showing strong nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity, characteristic of activation of the Wnt signaling pathway in solid pseudopapillary neoplasms; (D) Immunohistochemistry for alpha-1-antitrypsin demonstrating diffuse cytoplasmic positivity; (E) Immunohistochemistry for CD56 showing membranous positivity; (F) Immunohistochemistry for progesterone receptor showing nuclear positivity; (G) Immunohistochemistry for chromogranin showing negative staining, arguing against a neuroendocrine tumor; (H) Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) showing negative staining; (I) Immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin showing negative staining; (J) Immunohistochemistry for CD10 demonstrating membranous positivity.
in_text_mentions: a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, grade G1 (well differentiated), measuring 7 × 7.5 × 8 cm, confined to the pancreas, without lymphovascular or perineural invasion. All six resected lymph nodes were negative for malignancy, and the tumor was staged as pT4 pN0 pMx. The immunohistochemical profile supported the diagnosis, with nuclear positivity for β-catenin, reflecting activation of the Wnt signaling pathway, along with expression of alpha-1-antitrypsin, cluster of differentiation (CD)56, progesterone receptor, and CD10, consistent with the characteristic phenotype of this neoplasm (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: a one-day history of progressive sharp back pain, identified a 15 mm well-defined hypodense lesion in the pancreatic tail. At that time, further characterization with abdominal MRI was recommended, and the differential diagnosis included pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, SPN, and pancreatic blastoma. However, the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up, and the additional imaging was not performed. Given persistent symptoms, a non-contrast CT of the abdomen (Figure 1) was performed, which demonstrated a mass in the tail of the pancreas measuring 5.7 x 4.7 x 4.2 cm.

plate_findings.evidence: Histological appearance of solid neoplastic implant

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Panel A shows the solid pattern of a neoplastic implant in the great omentum, consistent with solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, as confirmed by the article context. B: Panel B demonstrates the characteristic pseudopapillary pattern of SPN, which is a key diagnostic feature mentioned in the caption. C: Panel C shows high-power histological views (200x) with cellular features characteristic of SPN, including specific nuclear and cytoplasmic morphology. D: Panel D demonstrates immunohistochemical expression of beta-catenin, a molecular finding used to support the diagnosis of SPN. E: Panel E shows positive staining for Cyclin D1, which is a relevant molecular marker in the context of SPN and pancreatic tumors. F: Panel F demonstrates CD10 expression, further supporting the histological diagnosis of SPN in the peritoneal implants.
panels.attribution_text: Nogueiro et al. Late Recurrence of Pancreatic Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm With Peritoneal Carcinomatosis Treated With Cytoreductive Surgery (CRS) and Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (HIPEC): A Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.31189. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histological appearance of one of the neoplastic implants in the great omentum Areas of solid (H&E, 100x) (A) and pseudopapillary patterns (H&E, 100x) (B) were seen, with associated fibrovascular stalks containing variable degree of myxoid change and hyalinization. Cells displayed ovoid nuclei with fine chromatin and characteristic longitudinal grooves; the cytoplasm was occasionally vacuolated and exhibited hyaline globules (H&E, 200x) (C). Nuclear and cytoplasmic expression of β-catenin was demonstrated by immunohistochemistry (100x) (D). Additionally, expression of cyclin D1 (100x) (E) and CD10 (100x) (F) was observed. Synaptophysin was expressed focally, whereas chromogranin expression was absent (not shown). H&E: hematoxylin and eosin stain
in_text_mentions: Intraoperatively, the peritoneal carcinomatosis index was 5. The patient was then submitted to CCRS combined with HIPEC with oxaliplatin (360mg/m2) and irinotecan (360mg/m2) at a temperature of 43ºC for 30 min. Histological examination confirmed the involvement of the great omentum, right diaphragmatic peritoneum and multiple peritoneal fragments by a pancreatic SPN (Figure 2).

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological features of the pancreatic solid pseudopapillary tumor: solid areas with monotonous cells with a hyalinized degenerative background (A); pseudopapillary areas with a myxoid hyalinized background (B-C); infiltration of tumor into the hilar splenic tissue (D).
in_text_mentions: Microscopically, the tumor showed heterogeneous architecture. It consisted of monotonous solid sheets of cells arranged around blood vessels, admixed with pseudo-papillary structures where the cells detached from the vascular core (Figure 8). Cytologically, the tumor cells displayed uniform nuclei, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and characteristic nuclear grooves. Mitotic figures were rare. The background demonstrated marked hyalinization and areas of hemorrhage, indicating degenerative changes (Figure 8).
